p3_archaeology_01: This season the excavation laid out 12 squares in the eastern area of the site, each 5 meters on a side, exposing a total of 300 square meters. It cleared 27 ash pits and 3 house remains and yielded about 4600 potsherds, 41 restorable pottery vessels and 65 ground stone tools. All finds have been numbered and placed in storage.
p3_archaeology_02: The stratigraphic record of excavation square 7 shows a topsoil layer about 20 centimeters thick, below which lies a layer of disturbed yellowish brown soil 35 centimeters thick. Further down is a grayish black cultural layer containing many charcoal flecks, reaching 140 centimeters below the surface at its deepest. Six charcoal samples were collected from this layer and have been sent to a laboratory for dating.
p3_archaeology_03: This painted pottery basin measures about 30 centimeters across the rim. Its walls are thin and the outer surface has been polished quite smooth. A continuous band of spiral patterns is painted in black around the upper belly, while the lower belly is left plain. A fine crack left during firing runs across the base, and several shallow finger impressions can still be seen on the inner wall.
p3_archaeology_04: A partly sunken house foundation has been exposed on the northern slope of the site. It is roughly circular in plan and about 5 meters in diameter, and its living floor was trampled so often that it became as hard as a thin shell. A hearth pit fired red sits in the center with 8 postholes spread around it, the sloping doorway faces southeast, and a ring of low earthen platform still remains along the wall.
p3_archaeology_05: Once the coordinates of the datum point have been measured with a total station, team members stretch strings and drive in stakes, dividing the ground into neat squares, and the excavation grid is complete. Digging then proceeds downward layer by layer, following changes in soil color and texture. After each layer is cleared, team members photograph and draw it and record where each artifact was found before digging further down.
p3_archaeology_06: At the field station, the first step for potsherds is cleaning. Technicians brush the soil off in clean water with soft brushes and then spread the pieces on bamboo mats to dry in the shade. Once fully dry, each sherd is marked with a number in an inconspicuous spot on its inner surface. Restorers then fit the pieces together one by one by matching decoration and broken edges, missing parts are filled in with plaster, and drawing and photography complete the work.
p3_archaeology_07: A few patterned potsherds were first found by a farmer turning over soil near a river, and he promptly reported them to the local cultural heritage office. After a week of coring, an archaeological team located a continuous cultural layer two meters below the ground. Further excavation confirmed that the spot is a Neolithic village site dating back about six thousand years.
p3_archaeology_08: In the third week of the excavation, as a student intern was scraping the ground level, a bone needle appeared under the trowel. It was less than 6 centimeters long, and the eye at its end was clearly visible. Clearing in that area stopped at once. Team members first photographed it and recorded its position, then wrapped it in tissue paper and placed it in a small numbered box.
p3_archaeology_09: Archaeological stratigraphy rests on a basic principle. Where the deposits have not been disturbed, lower layers formed earlier and upper layers formed later. As a result, within the same excavation square, artifacts from lower layers are usually older than those from upper layers, although later pits or animal burrows can upset this order.
p3_archaeology_10: A wall of earth about 1 meter wide is usually left between neighboring excavation squares, and it is called a balk. During excavation it serves as a walkway, and it also preserves the sections on all four sides. Archaeologists can compare the sections from several directions to check the layers, and only after the relationships among the layers are clear is the balk removed section by section.
p3_astronomy_01: Last night, a telescope with a 60 centimeter aperture at the observatory observed a variable star. The session ran from 9 in the evening until 3 in the morning, and 140 images were taken. During that time the brightness of the star rose and fell by about half a magnitude, with an estimated period of around 5 hours. Cloud cover was light that night, and the seeing stayed fairly good.
p3_astronomy_02: On the night of the meteor shower peak, an observing group recorded for 4 hours straight on a hillside outside the city. They counted 213 meteors in all, including 7 fireballs brighter than Venus and 19 that left trains. The hourly count was highest around 2 in the morning, at about 80 meteors.
p3_astronomy_03: This observatory stands on a summit 2400 meters above sea level, far from city lights. Its white dome is about 12 meters across and has a slit down the middle that can open and close. Under the dome sits a large reflecting telescope with a dark blue tube, and its base rests on a separate concrete pier that does not touch the floor.
p3_astronomy_04: Through a small telescope, Saturn looks pale yellow, and its rings circle the planet like the brim of a hat. A few parallel pale cloud bands are faintly visible on its disk. A thin dark gap in the rings divides them into an inner and an outer part. A bright point is often seen beside Saturn, and that point is its largest moon.
p3_astronomy_05: An hour before observing begins, staff open the dome so that the temperatures inside and outside can even out. Next, they use a bright star of known position to calibrate the pointing and set the focus. During the observing run, the telescope turns to each target in order from a prepared list and takes several images of each one. Before dawn, the data are copied to a server.
p3_astronomy_06: After a star like the Sun exhausts the hydrogen fuel in its core, it gradually enters old age. Its outer layers first swell into a red giant, growing hundreds of times larger. The outer gas is then slowly cast off, forming a glowing shell called a planetary nebula. The remaining core contracts into a white dwarf, which cools and dims over an immense span of time.
p3_astronomy_07: Last month, an amateur stargazer photographing the night sky noticed a bright star that had not been there before. A nearby observatory confirmed it with a spectrograph that same night, showing that it was a nova within the Milky Way whose brightness had risen more than a thousandfold in two days. Over the following weeks, it gradually faded again.
p3_astronomy_08: On a clear night last winter, a bright star passed just along the edge of the Moon, an event known as a grazing occultation. Twelve observing sites strung out along a line recorded it at the same time, and at several of them the starlight flickered on and off a number of times. From the timing of these flickers, researchers worked out the heights of several mountain peaks on the lunar limb.
p3_astronomy_09: Stars twinkle because their light, passing through the atmosphere, is disturbed by air currents of different temperatures, so its direction keeps bending very slightly. Stars are so far away that each looks almost like a single point, which makes the twinkling obvious. A planet appears as a tiny disk, and the jitter from its different parts averages out, so it looks comparatively steady.
p3_astronomy_10: The time the Moon takes to orbit the Earth once is almost the same as the time it takes to spin once on its axis, about 27 days each. As a result, the Moon always keeps the same face toward the Earth, and most of its far side cannot be seen directly from the Earth. This is called tidal locking, and it results from tidal forces slowing the rotation over a long period.
p3_bank_01: Last month, the branch opened 174 new personal accounts, most of them opened by new students from a nearby university. The counters handled about 140 transactions a day on average, with Mondays the busiest. The cash machines were refilled 9 times during the month, and the longest queue came on payday at the end of the month, lasting about half an hour.
p3_bank_02: At the start of the month, the branch put up a new table of interest rates, with the annual rate on one year fixed deposits cut by 10 basis points, the three year rate cut by 15 basis points, and the demand deposit rate unchanged. The new rates take effect on the 10th of this month, and fixed deposits already made are not affected by this change. In the week that followed, the branch received more than 60 inquiries.
p3_bank_03: The banking hall of the branch is small, with a ticket machine to the right of the entrance and three cash deposit and withdrawal machines against the wall on the left. In the middle of the hall stands a counter for filling in forms, with a few pens tied to it by thin strings. The service counter has four windows, and under each glass partition there is a small slot for passing cash and documents.
p3_bank_04: A passbook is a palm sized booklet with a cover of dark green card. The first page carries the account number and the date the account was opened, and every page after that is divided into rows. After each deposit or withdrawal, the teller puts the passbook into a printer, and the date and balance of the transaction are printed on a new line.
p3_bank_05: The first step in opening a savings account is to take a number from the ticket machine and wait in the waiting area to be called. When the number is called, the customer hands an identity document to the teller, who verifies it and enters the details. Next the customer signs a confirmation form and sets a password, and finally receives a bank card, with the whole process taking about twenty minutes.
p3_bank_06: After the branch closes for the day, each teller sorts and counts their cash by denomination and checks it item by item against the accounts of the day. Once the figures agree, the cash goes into numbered boxes, which two staff members seal together. At about seven in the evening a cash transport van reaches the branch, and after both sides sign the handover, the boxes are taken to the vault.
p3_bank_07: One morning during the summer holiday, a group of primary school pupils visited the branch with their teacher. The lobby manager showed the children a banknote counting machine and taught them to recognize the watermarks on banknotes. At the end, the children lined up at the counter, each made a small deposit with pocket money, and received their first passbook.
p3_bank_08: On a weekend morning, an elderly man came to the branch carrying a bag of coins, intending to change them into notes. The teller poured the coins into a sorting machine, which separated coins of different values and counted them one by one. There turned out to be 860 coins worth 347 yuan in total, and the man put the notes into his pocket and left looking pleased.
p3_bank_09: When a fixed deposit is withdrawn before maturity, the interest is calculated at the demand deposit rate on the day of withdrawal. Each certificate allows only one partial early withdrawal, the remaining balance still earns interest at the original rate, and the maturity date stays the same. If no action is taken when the deposit matures, the bank usually rolls it over automatically for the original term.
p3_bank_10: Transfers within the same bank usually arrive instantly, and transfers between banks on working days are normally completed within a few minutes. Large transfers between banks go through a separate clearing channel, which opens only on working days and pauses in the evenings and at weekends. Such transfers started during holidays are processed on the next working day.
p3_chemistry_01: In a titration, a conical flask held 25 milliliters of hydrochloric acid of unknown strength, and 2 drops of phenolphthalein were added. The first run used 24 milliliters of sodium hydroxide solution, and the next two used 25 milliliters each. All three runs ended at a pale pink color, and the technician used the last two results to calculate the concentration.
p3_chemistry_02: During the monthly inventory of the chemical storeroom, 412 bottles of reagents were counted, and liquids made up more than half of them. Fifteen bottles had passed their shelf life and were boxed separately to await disposal. Solids that readily absorb moisture were kept in a drying cabinet, where the humidity display read thirty percent. The results were entered into an electronic ledger the same day.
p3_chemistry_03: Copper sulfate pentahydrate is a blue crystalline substance whose grains form irregular lumps with a glassy luster. It dissolves quickly in water, giving a clear blue solution. When the crystals are heated, they gradually lose their water of crystallization and turn into a white powder, which becomes blue again on contact with water.
p3_chemistry_04: This organic chemistry lab has six fume hoods along its two side walls, each with a tempered glass sash that slides up and down. The benchtops are made of black resin that resists corrosion and feels slightly cool to the touch, and every bench station has a tap and a gas valve. A cabinet by the door holds goggles and gloves, and an eyewash station stands in the corner.
p3_chemistry_05: Purifying crude salt takes three steps, dissolving, filtering, and evaporating. The crude salt is first placed in a beaker, and it fully dissolves once water is added and stirred in. The mixture is then filtered through a funnel lined with filter paper, which holds back the sand and mud. Finally the filtrate is heated in an evaporating dish, the heating stops once plenty of crystals appear, and the remaining heat drives off the last of the water.
p3_chemistry_06: To grow an alum crystal, enough alum is first dissolved in hot water, forming a saturated solution. As the solution cools, many small crystals settle on the bottom of the cup, and a neatly shaped one is chosen as a seed. The seed is hung on a fine thread in freshly made saturated solution and left undisturbed in a cool place. As the water slowly evaporates, the seed grows larger over several days.
p3_chemistry_07: At the end of last term, a school laboratory found a bottle of white powder with a blurred label while clearing out an old cabinet. A technician dissolved a small amount in water, a white precipitate formed when silver nitrate solution was added, and a flame test gave a yellow flame. From these results the powder was identified as sodium chloride, and the bottle was then relabeled.
p3_chemistry_08: Recently, a team at a materials research institute completed weathering tests on a batch of new thermal insulation coatings. The sample panels had sat on outdoor exposure racks for a year, through heat, heavy rain, and freezing. Tests showed only slight chalking on the coating surface, and the insulating performance had dropped by less than five percent.
p3_chemistry_09: Aluminum is chemically more reactive than iron, yet it does not corrode easily in air. This is because a dense film of aluminum oxide quickly forms on its surface and seals the metal underneath from the air. Rust on iron, by contrast, is loose and porous, so water and oxygen keep seeping in, and iron objects rust away layer by layer.
p3_chemistry_10: Sugar and ethanol dissolve easily in water because their molecules, like water molecules, are polar. Fat molecules are almost nonpolar, so fats hardly dissolve in water but do dissolve in gasoline. This pattern is often summed up by saying that like dissolves like, meaning that the more similar a solute and a solvent are in structure, the more readily they dissolve in each other.
p3_computing_01: As of this Monday, machine room 3 had 168 servers in service spread across 24 racks, with an average inlet air temperature of 22 degrees Celsius. This inspection found abnormal fan speeds on 2 servers, an engineer replaced the fans on the spot, and every indicator for the remaining equipment was within the normal range.
p3_computing_02: Version 6 of this bookkeeping software was released in March this year, and since then 4 updates have been pushed out, fixing 37 known problems and adding 2 reporting functions. The latest update was completed at the end of October, the installation package is 12 megabytes smaller than the previous version, and startup time has dropped from about 5 seconds to about 3 seconds.
p3_computing_03: In the machine room on the first basement level, four rows of black racks stand in neat lines, with transparent panels between them separating cold aisles from hot aisles. Yellow cable trays run below the ceiling, two precision air conditioners stand by the wall and give off a low hum while running, and the entrance is fitted with an access control gate and a shoe cover machine.
p3_computing_04: This rack server takes up two units of height, its front panel holds twelve drive bays, and each bay has a green status light beside it. Two power supply units and four network ports sit side by side on the back of the chassis, and lifting the top cover reveals two processors under silver heat sinks, with memory modules lined up neatly on both sides.
p3_computing_05: The rollout of a new version proceeds in three stages. The first stage verifies every function in a test environment, the second deploys the version on only five percent of the servers and watches them for two days in a row, and once no anomalies are found, the third stage extends it to all servers, with the switchover finished in the early hours of a weekend.
p3_computing_06: When new servers arrive, the storekeeper checks the serial numbers and attaches asset labels. The installers slide each server onto its rails, fix it at units 18 and 19 of the rack, and connect the power and network cables. Once the startup check passes, the operations staff install the base software and enter the server in the asset ledger, and the whole racking procedure takes about two hours.
p3_computing_07: Early on Tuesday morning, one of the utility power feeds to a data center suddenly failed, the uninterruptible power supply took over at once, and the diesel generators started within a minute. No server lost power during the whole episode, the staff on duty noted the time of each switchover, and once utility power returned, they moved the load back to the original line.
p3_computing_08: A logistics company updated its warehouse management software last month, and on the second day after the update several branch sites reported garbled characters on printed labels. Technicians traced the problem to the font configuration in the new version, rolled the software back to the old version that afternoon, and released a corrected version three days later, after which printing returned to normal.
p3_computing_09: The relative humidity in a machine room is generally kept between forty and sixty percent. When humidity is too low the air is dry and static electricity builds up easily, which can damage electronic components, and when it is too high, water droplets tend to condense on equipment surfaces, so machine rooms are usually fitted with both humidifiers and dehumidifiers.
p3_computing_10: Software version numbers are often expressed as three groups of digits, where the first group goes up by one after major changes, the second goes up by one when new features are added, and the third goes up by one only when problems are fixed, with the other two left unchanged. From the change in the version number, maintainers can roughly judge the scope of an update.
p3_construction_01: On Wednesday this week, the concrete pour for the twelfth floor slab of Building 5 was completed, using 186 cubic meters of concrete. The pour began at seven in the morning and lasted about nine hours. Twelve sets of test cubes were taken on site and sent to a laboratory for strength testing. The temperature rose to 29 degrees Celsius that afternoon, and the newly poured slab was covered with plastic sheeting to hold in moisture.
p3_construction_06: A static load test of the river bridge was carried out on October 20 with 16 trucks loaded with sand and gravel, each weighing about 35 tonnes in total. The trucks drove onto the deck in four groups and parked at marked positions. The largest downward deflection, measured at the midpoint of the main span, was 28 millimeters, and the deck returned almost to its original position once the load was removed.
p3_construction_02: This stone arch bridge spans the river in the middle of the town and is about 40 meters long. It is built of bluestone, with a large semicircular arch in the center and a smaller arch on each side to let floodwater through. Low stone railings line both edges of the deck, and lotus patterns are carved into their panels. At the approach to the bridge there are a few steps, worn very smooth.
p3_construction_07: A tower crane stands in the middle of the site, about 60 meters tall, its mast built from square steel frame sections. At the top a long jib reaches out to one side, and several concrete counterweights hang from the shorter arm on the other side. The operator cab sits just below the top, with glass on all four sides. At night a red warning light glows at the tip of the jib.
p3_construction_03: Construction of this apartment building began with surveying and setting out. Excavators then dug the foundation pit to a depth of 6 meters. After a base layer of concrete was poured at the bottom of the pit, workers tied the steel reinforcement and set up the formwork, then poured the pile caps and ground beams. Only after the foundation was finished and the soil backfilled did the main structure begin to go up floor by floor.
p3_construction_08: To build this bridge, whose deck hangs from stay cables, the crew first drilled bored piles into the riverbed and built the foundations of the two main towers. The towers then rose section by section to 120 meters. Next, steel box girders were assembled outward from both sides of each tower in balanced pairs, and a pair of stay cables was hung after each new segment. Once the girders from the two sides met in the middle of the river, paving of the deck began right away.
p3_construction_04: Yesterday morning, a flatbed truck carrying steel beams sank into a muddy hole left by the rain at the site entrance. The driver tried several times but could not drive it out, and the concrete mixer trucks behind it were stuck on the road as well. A wheel loader was brought over and pulled the flatbed out with a steel cable. Afterward, workers spread a layer of crushed stone over the entrance.
p3_construction_09: At the end of last month, the pedestrian overpass on the east side of the city, in use for thirty years, was taken down. At one in the morning the road beneath it was temporarily closed. Workers cut the span into four sections, and two large cranes lifted them one by one onto transport trucks. The whole job took less than six hours, and the road reopened before the morning rush hour.
p3_construction_05: The steel and concrete of a bridge expand in heat and contract in cold. To accommodate this movement, expansion joints are placed at intervals along the deck. In the summer heat the gaps narrow, and when it cools in winter they open up again. Without expansion joints, the deck could be squeezed until it buckles upward or cracks.
p3_construction_10: Concrete is very strong in compression, but its tensile strength is only about one tenth of its compressive strength. Steel bars are good at carrying tension, and the two materials expand by very similar amounts when heated. In practice, steel bars are usually placed on the tension side of beams and floor slabs, so that the members are less likely to crack under load.
p3_cooking_01: This canteen sold 412 boxed lunches at noon on Wednesday. Braised chicken was the most popular dish with 156 portions sold, tomato and egg stir fry sold 98, and the vegetable platter sold 73. About 12 kilograms of rice were left over, the kitchen finished all cleaning before two in the afternoon, and dinner preparation started at three.
p3_cooking_02: A recipe for homestyle braised pork lists the main quantities. It uses 500 grams of pork belly, 30 grams of rock sugar, 20 milliliters of light soy sauce, 10 milliliters of dark soy sauce, two star anise and five slices of ginger. Enough water is added to cover the meat, the pot simmers over low heat for about 60 minutes, and the dish serves four people.
p3_cooking_03: The back kitchen of this restaurant is about twelve meters long. Four gas stoves stand in a row along the wall under a wide exhaust hood, and a stainless steel worktable sits in the middle with cutting boards and metal basins on its lower shelf. The door to the cold room is at the far end, the floor is laid with nonslip tiles, and a drainage channel runs along the wall.
p3_cooking_04: This cast iron casserole weighs about four kilograms. Its body is deep red, and the inside has a cream colored enamel coating. The underside of the lid has a ring of raised dots that let condensed steam drip back into the pot. The two handles are wide and the base is flat, so the pot works on a gas stove or in an oven.
p3_cooking_05: To make dumplings by hand, the cook first kneads flour and warm water into a smooth dough and lets it rest under a damp cloth for half an hour. Minced pork and chopped cabbage are then mixed into a filling. The dough is rolled into a rope, cut into small pieces and rolled out into round wrappers, which are filled and pinched shut. Finally the dumplings are boiled until they float.
p3_cooking_06: Baking a chiffon cake goes through several stages. Egg yolks are first whisked with milk and vegetable oil, and cake flour is sifted in. Separately, the egg whites are beaten while sugar is added in three portions. The two mixtures are then gently folded together, poured into a pan and baked at 160 degrees for about 50 minutes. As soon as it comes out of the oven, the cake is turned upside down to cool.
p3_cooking_07: Last Saturday evening, the kitchen of a noodle shop suddenly lost power. The bone broth on the stove had to be taken off the heat for a while, and several cooks kept cutting ingredients by flashlight. The manager temporarily switched the menu to cold noodles and dressed side dishes. Power came back forty minutes later, dinner service went on as usual, and the shop served more than sixty tables that night.
p3_cooking_08: The cooking class of a vocational school held a cooking contest at the end of the year. Twenty students were divided into five groups, and each group made one hot dish and one pastry within ninety minutes. The judges scored knife work, heat control and plating. A flower carved from a radish by one student drew a crowd. In the end, the steamed fish of the third group received the highest score.
p3_cooking_09: Dough rises because yeast breaks down sugar and produces carbon dioxide. Once the gas is trapped in the gluten network, the dough expands and turns light. Yeast is most active at around 28 degrees, and fermentation slows noticeably when the temperature is too low. Too much salt also holds back the yeast, so salt and yeast are usually added separately when the dough is mixed.
p3_cooking_10: In deep frying, the oil temperature determines the texture. Oil at around 150 degrees suits thicker pieces of meat because it lets the inside cook through slowly. At 180 degrees the outer layer turns crisp quickly, which suits fries and tempura. When the oil gets too hot, it gives off thick smoke and the surface of the food easily burns black.
p3_ecology_01: On the morning of October 12, a survey team laid out 6 transects in the wetland on the east bank, each 500 meters long. Observers recorded 23 species of waterbirds, about 1400 birds in total. Grey herons made up the largest share, with 310 of them standing in the shallows. Water clarity was 42 centimeters, slightly lower than the month before.
p3_ecology_06: This quarter the infrared cameras captured 860 usable photos across 12 sites. Wild boar appeared most often, with 214 detections. Muntjacs were photographed 97 times, mostly active in the early morning. Leopard cats were recorded for the first time at 3 other sites, and all of those photos were taken at night.
p3_ecology_02: This mixed forest lies on the north slope of a valley and covers about 80 hectares. The upper canopy is dominated by oaks and Masson pines, while the lower layer holds dense patches of azaleas and ferns. A seasonal stream runs through the woods, and in the rainy season its water can reach half a meter deep. Fallen leaves lie in a thick layer on the ground and feel very soft underfoot.
p3_ecology_07: This lake on the plateau is long and narrow, stretching about 7 kilometers from north to south. Its water has a faint bluish green tint because of its high salt content, and a layer of white salt crust covers the gravel along the shore. On the east side lies a gently sloping meadow, slightly higher than the lake surface, which fills with small yellow flowers every summer.
p3_ecology_03: Researchers first drove wooden stakes into the four corners of the plot, then used rope to mark out a square 20 meters on each side. Next they measured every tree with a trunk diameter over 5 centimeters at breast height, and hung a numbered tag on each trunk. When the measuring was done, the data were entered into a spreadsheet, and the plot location was marked on a map.
p3_ecology_08: An abandoned farm field gradually turns back into forest. In the first few years, the ground is covered with annual weeds. Then perennial herbs and shrubs begin to dominate, and seeds carried in by birds sprout there as well. After about twenty years, pioneer trees join into small patches of woodland, and saplings that tolerate shade then grow up beneath them.
p3_ecology_04: In early summer last year, a flock of egrets flew into the reed beds at the river mouth to build nests. At first the ranger saw only a dozen or so birds, but the number of nests later grew to more than 60. In July the chicks left their nests one after another and learned to forage in the shallow water. When autumn arrived, the whole flock moved away to the south.
p3_ecology_09: Last month, three days of heavy rain made the small river below the mountain rise sharply. After the flood receded, monitoring staff found large numbers of dead branches that had washed up on a sandbar downstream. Two stretches of the bank collapsed, and willows that had grown along the edge fell into the channel. A nearby otter den was also filled with silt.
p3_ecology_05: Reeds in a wetland slow the flow of water, letting sediment gradually settle out. Their rhizomes spread and interlace in the mud, holding the soil along the banks firmly in place. Dense reed beds give small fish and waterbirds places to hide, and they also absorb excess nutrients from the water, so they are often seen as a sign of a healthy wetland.
p3_ecology_10: The reeds in a wetland have dense roots, which hold the soft mud in place and slow the erosion of the banks by flowing water. Reed beds also give many water birds places to nest and shelter, and every spring flocks of wild ducks lay their eggs among them. Dead reed stems sink to the bottom and slowly decompose, providing nutrients for small aquatic organisms.
p3_energy_01: The daily operating report of a solar power station on the north side of the city shows that last Wednesday the station generated about thirty thousand kilowatt hours, eight percent more than the day before. Sunshine added up to 7 hours, the panel surface temperature peaked at 31 degrees Celsius, and all 12 inverters at the station ran normally, with no shutdowns recorded.
p3_energy_02: An office building with three floors used 8600 kilowatt hours of electricity in October, with air conditioning taking about forty percent and lighting about twenty percent. Compared with September, total use fell by 900 kilowatt hours, mostly from air conditioning, because temperatures dropped after the middle of the month and the air conditioners ran for noticeably shorter hours each day.
p3_energy_03: The small hydropower station in the valley sits right beside a river, and its powerhouse is a gray building of two floors with a roof of dark tiles. Inside, two hydroelectric generating units are installed side by side, a row of control cabinets stands next to them, and each cabinet door carries an equipment number, with the date of the latest overhaul marked below it.
p3_energy_04: At the gate of the residential compound there is a power distribution room with pale green walls and a yellow warning sign hanging on its iron door. Three transformers stand in the middle of the room, surrounded by neatly arranged switch cabinets, the floor is covered with black insulating mats, and a fire extinguisher and an inspection logbook sit in one corner.
p3_energy_05: Before a unit at a gas power plant starts up, the operators first check the fuel lines and the cooling water pressure, then engage the turning gear so that the rotor turns slowly. After ignition the speed rises step by step, the unit is connected to the grid when it reaches rated speed, and the load is then raised little by little until the output reaches the value set by the dispatchers.
p3_energy_06: On the day of the line maintenance, the dispatch center first ordered a power cut, and the substations at both ends opened their switches right away. After reaching the site, the maintenance crew tested for voltage and attached grounding wires, then replaced the aged insulators. When the work was finished, the crew removed the grounding wires and counted their tools, and power returned to the line in the evening.
p3_energy_07: A strong wind snapped a tree branch beside a power line on the outskirts of town, the branch fell across the conductors, and three nearby villages lost power at once. A repair crew reached the scene 40 minutes later, cleared the branch and checked the conductors, and at about 7 that evening all three villages had their power back.
p3_energy_08: During a routine patrol, an inspector noticed that a joint on a disconnect switch at a substation was running hot, and an infrared thermometer showed it to be 20 degrees Celsius warmer than the neighboring joints. That evening the maintenance team scheduled an outage to deal with it and replaced the joint bolts, and when it was measured again the next day, the temperature was back to normal.
p3_energy_09: The frequency of a power grid shows whether generation and consumption are in balance. When the load rises suddenly and generation fails to keep up, the frequency falls, and in the opposite case it rises. To keep the frequency stable, dispatchers assign some generating units to adjust their output at any moment, and such units are usually called frequency regulation units.
p3_energy_10: Many cities charge households different electricity prices at different times of day, with daytime and early evening counted as peak hours at relatively high prices, and the period from 11 at night to 7 the next morning counted as low demand hours at lower prices. Some families therefore run their washing machines and water heaters at night, and their monthly electricity bills go down as a result.
p3_environment_01: This residential compound collected 3200 kilograms of kitchen waste in October, along with 1150 kilograms of recyclables and 4600 kilograms of other waste. Compared with September, kitchen waste rose by about twenty percent and other waste fell by 300 kilograms, which the supervisor credited mainly to the two newly added collection points.
p3_environment_02: On Monday morning this week, a water quality monitor collected one water sample at each of three sections of the river. Dissolved oxygen was 8 milligrams per liter at the upstream section and 7 at the middle section, dropping to 5 downstream, the water temperature at all three was around 18 degrees Celsius, and the turbidity at all three sections was slightly lower than last month.
p3_environment_03: The waste sorting kiosk at the gate of the compound is a small hut with a canopy, and along its front stand four bins of different colors, which are green, blue, red and gray. Simple pictures are printed on the lids, a wash basin is fitted on one side of the kiosk, and at night the light under the canopy stays on until ten.
p3_environment_04: An automatic water quality monitoring buoy floats in the middle of the reservoir, shaped like a big orange spinning top about one and a half meters across. A solar panel and a short antenna are mounted on top, and the probe at the bottom reaches half a meter below the surface, measuring water temperature and acidity every four hours and sending the data by wireless signal back to the station building on shore.
p3_environment_05: Collecting water samples follows a fixed procedure. On reaching the sampling point, the monitor rinses the sample bottle three times with river water, and next pushes the bottle about thirty centimeters below the surface to fill it. The labeled samples go into a cooler to stay cold, are taken back to the laboratory the same day, and are analyzed within 48 hours.
p3_environment_06: The energy saving retrofit of the office building was done floor by floor. On each floor, the workers took down the old fluorescent tubes, replaced them with light emitting diode lamps, and at the same time installed sensor switches in the corridor. After the whole building was finished, the property management also set the lowest summer temperature for the air conditioning at 26 degrees, and the electricity bill in the first month after the retrofit was nearly one third lower than in the same period last year.
p3_environment_07: Early in the morning the day before yesterday, more than ten bags of unsorted waste were piled beside the bins at the collection point by the river, holding leftover food as well as waste paper and plastic bottles. That same day the supervisor put up sorting diagrams in the stairwells of several nearby buildings, and when checking again three days later, found that the waste at the same spot had mostly been sorted.
p3_environment_08: In the middle of August, monitoring data from a small reservoir showed that algae in the water multiplied rapidly within a week, and parts of the surface turned green. Technicians rushed to the site to take samples and judged that this was related to days of high temperatures and fallen leaves washed down from upstream, so they cleared the floating debris and increased the volume of water exchanged, and half a month later the water was clear again.
p3_environment_09: In most cities, large bones and shells are not counted as kitchen waste but are classed as other waste. Such items are hard and difficult to crush or ferment, and mixing them into kitchen waste can damage the processing equipment. Likewise, used paper napkins are treated as other waste because they are hard to recycle.
p3_environment_10: Many appliances remain on standby after being switched off, and as long as the plug stays in, they keep consuming a small amount of electricity. The standby power of a television is usually only a few watts, but over a year it can add up to twenty or thirty kilowatt hours, so some households make a habit of using power strips with switches and cutting off a whole row of sockets at once before bed.
p3_factory_01: Yesterday, Injection Molding Workshop 2 produced 120 thousand bottle caps over three shifts. An inspector sampled 500 of them and found burrs on the edges of 5. Equipment downtime for the day added up to 40 minutes, mainly because a heater band on one molding machine failed. After the part was replaced, production returned to normal at two in the afternoon.
p3_factory_06: Throughout October, the quality department sampled 3200 motor housings and found 41 defective pieces. Of these, 23 were out of dimensional tolerance, 15 had surface scratches, and 3 contained gas pores. Compared with September, the defect rate fell by about one third. All the defective pieces were sent back to the machining section to be dealt with.
p3_factory_02: This assembly workshop is about 120 meters long, with a row of skylights along the roof. A slowly moving conveyor belt runs down the middle, with more than twenty workstations lined up along its two sides. Tool racks and work lights hang above the workstations, and yellow lines on the floor mark out the walkways. Boxes of parts waiting to be assembled are stacked in one corner, and forklifts weave back and forth between them.
p3_factory_07: This welding robot is mounted on a base beside the production line. Its arm has six joints, and a welding torch is fitted at the end. The work area is enclosed by an orange safety fence, with dark shading curtains hanging all around. A control cabinet beside it has a display screen, and below the screen is a red emergency stop button.
p3_factory_03: Glass bottle production begins with batching, in which quartz sand and soda ash are mixed in set proportions and fed into a furnace. The raw materials melt into molten glass at a high temperature of about 1500 degrees Celsius and are then cut into gobs of equal size. Each gob drops into a mold and is blown into the shape of a bottle. The bottles cool slowly in an annealing oven, and those that pass inspection are boxed and stored.
p3_factory_08: In the spinning workshop, raw cotton is first opened and cleaned to remove impurities and short fibers. A carding machine then combs the fibers into a thin web and gathers it into a thick sliver. The sliver is drawn out gradually through the drawing and roving stages, and is finally twisted into yarn on a spinning frame and wound onto bobbins.
p3_factory_04: During the night shift last Friday, the case sealer at the end of the packaging line suddenly jammed, and cartons on the conveyor quickly backed up in a row. The shift leader pressed the stop button and opened the guard with a maintenance worker to check. It turned out that the paper core of a tape roll had come loose and wound into the rollers. Once it was cleared, the line, which had been stopped for about twenty minutes, started running again.
p3_factory_09: This summer, the biscuit production line at a food factory was refitted. The old gas tunnel oven was replaced with an electric one, and the line was shut down for two full weeks during the changeover. Once the new oven came into use, the biscuits browned more evenly, and hourly output rose from 800 to 950 kilograms. The workshop was also noticeably cooler than before.
p3_factory_05: In many factories, first article inspection means that when production of each batch begins, the first finished piece is checked in full. Only if its dimensions and appearance both pass does the batch go into full production. This catches problems with machine setup or materials early, and keeps the whole batch from ending up with the same defect.
p3_factory_10: Precision parts usually have their dimensions measured in a constant temperature room kept at 20 degrees Celsius all year round. This is because metal expands when heated. A steel piece 100 millimeters long grows by about 1 micrometer for every 1 degree Celsius rise in temperature. For parts with tolerances of only a few micrometers, such a change is enough to alter the inspection result.
p3_farm_01: This year the field east of the village was planted with 12 mu of maize, sown in late April and harvested from mid September. When the harvest was in, it had yielded about ten thousand jin of maize, more than 800 jin per mu on average, the best crop in five years. Most of the dried maize was sold to the buying station in the town.
p3_farm_02: The seedling greenhouse held 2400 seedling trays, and by the fifth day after sowing more than ninety percent of the seeds had come up. Inside, the daytime temperature was kept at around 25 degrees and did not fall below 15 at night. By the twentieth day the seedlings stood about 12 centimeters tall on average, ready to be transplanted to the fields.
p3_farm_03: The rice paddies at the foot of the hill are divided by earth ridges into a dozen or so plots of different sizes, and a canal runs along the edge of the fields, fed all year round by water from a reservoir upstream. Grass and a few clumps of wild chrysanthemums grow on the ridges, and several egrets often feed in the flooded fields. Near the entrance to the village stands a small shed piled with farm tools.
p3_farm_04: The granary at the edge of the village is built of red brick, with its outer walls coated in white lime and its roof covered with gray tiles. The door is made of thick wood and sits half a meter above the ground, with three steps built in front of it. Inside, the floor is lined with wooden boards, and several small windows in the walls let air through and keep out the damp.
p3_farm_05: Before spring sowing, the farmers first loosen the soil with a rotary tiller and then rake the surface level. Next they open furrows 60 centimeters apart, scatter the seeds evenly into them and cover them with a thin layer of soil. After sowing, the soil is pressed firm with a roller, and finally water is run once along the furrows.
p3_farm_06: When the wheat is ripe, a combine harvester drives into the field from the headland, cutting and threshing as it goes. Once the grain tank of the harvester is full, the grain is unloaded onto a tractor waiting at the edge of the field. The tractor carries the grain to the drying yard, where it is spread out to dry for two or three days, and once its moisture has dropped it is bagged and sent to the grain depot.
p3_farm_07: On a morning during the autumn harvest, a tractor sank into the mud in a low patch at the edge of a field, its rear wheels digging deeper with every turn. The driver found two planks to put under the wheels and called over a neighbor, who brought another tractor to help tow it. The two vehicles were linked with a steel cable, and in less than ten minutes the stuck tractor had been pulled free.
p3_farm_08: In mid July, the agricultural technology station of the town brought a crop spraying drone to test spreading fertilizer over the rice fields of the cooperative. The drone flew back and forth along a preset route, covering about 20 mu on each run. By the end of the morning all 200 mu had been covered, and the farmers watching from the ridges stayed for a long time.
p3_farm_09: Farmland in this area follows a rotation of wheat and maize, giving two harvests a year. Wheat is sown in October and harvested in June of the following year, and maize is sown straight into the wheat stubble as soon as the wheat harvest ends. The maize ripens in September, and after it is harvested the land rests briefly before a new round of wheat sowing begins.
p3_farm_10: Once rice plants have produced enough tillers, the water in the paddy is drained and the field surface is left to dry for five to seven days, a practice known as field drying. Drying lets air into the soil, encourages the roots to grow deeper, and reduces the unproductive tillers that would otherwise form later. When the drying is over, the field is flooded again with shallow water.
p3_festival_01: This year the Lantern Festival show ran for 6 days in the park on the west side of the city, with more than 2300 lanterns on display. One dragon lantern group stretched 28 meters and was made of more than 400 small lanterns strung together. The riddle area prepared 800 lantern riddles, and about forty thousand visits were recorded on the closing night, roughly thirty percent more than the same period last year.
p3_festival_02: During the temple fair from the second to the sixth day of the first lunar month, 312 stalls were set up along both sides of the old street, and nearly half of them sold snacks. At its longest, the line in front of the sugar painting stall stretched more than 40 meters. The organizers counted about 19000 sticks of candied haws sold over the five days, and the stage hosted 26 folk performances, with the lion dance and stilt walking the most popular.
p3_festival_03: The head used in a lion dance has a frame of thin bamboo strips covered with several layers of gauze paper. A small round mirror is fixed at the center of the forehead, and the two large eyes can blink up and down. The mouth opens and closes by means of a pull cord, colorful pompoms cover the top of the head and both cheeks, and the whole head weighs just over one and a half kilograms.
p3_festival_04: The old street where the temple fair is held is no more than three hundred meters long, and its bluestone paving has been trodden to a shine. Red lanterns hang thickly under the eaves of the wooden buildings on both sides, and a decorated archway has been put up at the entrance to the street. On the small square in the middle stand several rows of benches facing a temporary stage, while the far end of the street is given over to stalls selling pinwheels and clay figurines.
p3_festival_05: The frame of a revolving horse lantern is bound by a craftsman from thin bamboo strips into a hexagon. After translucent tissue paper is pasted around the sides, a spindle with a vane wheel is mounted inside the lantern, with cut paper silhouettes of riders and horses attached to it. Finally a small candle is lit on the base, the rising hot air turns the vane wheel, and the silhouettes circle round and round across the paper without stopping.
p3_festival_06: On the day before the Dragon Boat Festival, the older villagers boil bamboo leaves in a large pot until soft, lift them out and wipe them dry one by one. Next, they pack soaked glutinous rice and red dates into leaves rolled into funnels, press the filling firm, fold the leaves shut and tie them tightly with cotton thread. Finally, they stack the rice dumplings in the pot and simmer them over a low flame for three hours.
p3_festival_07: Halfway through a moon viewing gathering on the night of the Mid Autumn Festival, the colored lights along the river all went out at once, and the whole street lost power for more than twenty minutes. Several stall keepers set flashlights and candles on the bridge railings, and people simply sat on the steps to look at the moon. When the power came back, a round of applause rose along the bank.
p3_festival_08: On the night of the Lantern Festival, more than half of the five hundred riddles hung along the riddle corridor had been solved by a little after nine. A middle school boy tore down seventeen riddle slips in one go and exchanged them for a big bag of prizes. Staff brought two more boxes of spare riddle slips from the storeroom at short notice, and the corridor stayed lively until late at night.
p3_festival_09: The Double Ninth Festival falls on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month. In ancient times nine was regarded as a yang number, and because two nines meet on this day, the festival came to be called Chongyang, meaning double yang. Its customs are mostly tied to climbing heights. People climb hills together, admire chrysanthemums and eat a layered festival cake, and in some places the cake is made with nine layers.
p3_festival_10: In a traditional dragon boat race, victory goes to the crew that seizes the flag at the finish. Each boat carries more than twenty paddlers. The drummer at the bow sets the rhythm, the paddlers dip their paddles together on the beat, and the helmsman at the stern steers. Even if a boat crosses the finish line first, it does not win unless it pulls down the flag.
p3_film_01: Shooting day 12 started at 5 in the morning and wrapped at 9 at night. The crew completed 4 scenes at the old railway station and shot 63 takes in all, including a farewell scene on the platform that was reshot 11 times. On the continuity sheet, 41 takes were marked as usable, and most of the remaining 22 were dropped because of excessive noise on location.
p3_film_02: The rough cut of the film ran 2 hours 18 minutes, and after three rounds of revision it was trimmed to 1 hour 52 minutes. The film contains 1460 shots, averaging about four and a half seconds each, and music covers four tenths of the running time. There are as many as 1105 subtitle entries, each of which has been proofread twice.
p3_film_03: The clapperboard used by the film crew consists of a black wooden board slightly larger than a textbook and a clapstick. The face of the board is divided into several columns by white lines, with the scene and take numbers marked in chalk. The clapstick is hinged to the top of the board and painted with black and white diagonal stripes, and it gives a crisp crack when snapped shut. Editors rely on that sound to line up the audio with the picture.
p3_film_04: The projection booth sits high in the back wall of the auditorium and is only about the size of a bed. Two small square windows open in its wall, one for the light beam to pass through and one for watching the screen. An old film projector stands in the room, a dozen or so round film cans are stacked on the iron rack beside it, and the air always smells of machine oil mixed with dust.
p3_film_05: The director walks the actors through their positions, and based on this the camera crew lays the dolly track and sets the camera position. The lighting crew then adjusts the angle and brightness of the lamps, and a full rehearsal with the camera follows. Once every department has confirmed that all is ready, the camera starts rolling and the slate is clapped right away, and only then does the take officially begin.
p3_film_06: In the editing room, the editor first arranges the shots by scene and assembles a long rough cut, then trims it and adjusts the pacing over repeated viewings to arrive at a fine cut. Once the picture is locked, the colorist unifies the color tone of the whole film and the sound mixer completes the mix. Finally, subtitles are added and a print for screening is output.
p3_film_07: On the morning the seaside scene was shot, the tide came in half an hour earlier than forecast, and the dolly track laid on the beach was soon soaked. The crew had to move the camera position back twenty meters and switch to handheld shooting. The actors finished the performance in seawater up to their ankles, and that take was later cut into the final film without any changes.
p3_film_08: The last outdoor film screening before winter was held on the playground of the village primary school. The projectionist had hung the screen by early evening, and by nightfall the playground was full of villagers who had brought stools. Halfway through the film, the projector bulb suddenly burned out. The projectionist fitted a spare bulb in the dark, and ten minutes later the picture lit up again.
p3_film_09: When a scene of two people talking is filmed, the camera generally stays on one side of the line joining them. This invisible line is called the axis. As long as the camera does not cross it, one person always faces right in the frame and the other always faces left, so the audience does not lose track of where the characters are. Once the axis is crossed, the two suddenly appear to swap directions.
p3_film_10: Film is projected at 24 frames per second, and each frame is a still photograph. Because of persistence of vision, the sequence of still images blends into smooth motion in the eyes of the audience. To reduce flicker, the shutter blades of the projector flash each frame on the screen twice, so what the audience actually sees is 48 flashes of light per second.
p3_fishery_01: At five in the morning, this fishing boat returned to port after six days at sea. It unloaded about 3200 kilograms of iced hairtail, about 900 kilograms of pomfret, and eleven baskets of swimming crabs. Weighing at the quay took nearly two hours, and the buying price of hairtail that day was two yuan per kilogram higher than the week before.
p3_fishery_02: The tally sheet of the port management station showed 147 fishing boat arrivals this week, 23 more than the week before. Trawlers accounted for 91 arrivals, and gillnetters and carrier vessels for the other 56. Sailings stopped for a day on Wednesday because of strong wind, and Friday saw the largest landings, at about 58 tonnes.
p3_fishery_03: The fishing port sits in a half moon bay, and the breakwater on its east side extends about three hundred meters into the sea. More than a hundred wooden fishing boats painted blue are moored in the harbor basin, with faded pennants hanging from their masts. Salt frost coats the outer walls of a row of low cold stores along the shore, fish scales lie scattered in the cracks between the flagstones of the quay, and the air carries a faint salty smell of fish.
p3_fishery_04: The trawler moored at berth three has a steel hull about 38 meters long, painted dark green. Two winches and a huge gantry frame stand on the rear deck, and the net is wound on a drum. Below deck lies the fish hold, its walls lined with insulation panels, able to take more than twenty tonnes of crushed ice and catch.
p3_fishery_05: Every morning at dawn, dock workers tip the freshly landed catch onto a long sorting table. They sort the fish by species and size into different plastic crates and pick out any damaged ones. The sorted fish are weighed and logged crate by crate, covered with a layer of crushed ice, and moved by forklift into a cold store to chill. After the wholesale market opens, the fish are loaded onto refrigerated trucks and sent out.
p3_fishery_06: Drying eels takes roughly three stages. Fishing families first split the eels open along the back, remove the innards and backbone, and wash them clean in seawater. The second stage is rubbing them with salt and curing them for half a day, then spreading each body open with bamboo strips. Finally they hang on wooden racks by the sea for three to five days of wind and sun, and once the flesh turns firm and translucent, they are taken down and tied into bundles.
p3_fishery_07: On its way back to port, a small fishing boat had its propeller fouled by an abandoned fishing net and lost power, drifting at sea. The skipper radioed another fishing boat working nearby. Two hours later the other boat arrived and towed the vessel back to port with a rope, a diver then cleared away the tangled net, and the three crew members on board were all unharmed.
p3_fishery_08: On the first morning after the fishing festival this year, the quay of the fishing port was much busier than usual. More than forty boats came in one after another, and fish traders had been waiting by the berths since before dawn. A boatload of freshly unloaded swimming crabs sold out within half an hour, the buyers sent two extra refrigerated trucks at short notice, and the quay did not grow quiet until noon.
p3_fishery_09: After sea fish are caught, the enzymes in their bodies stay active, and at room temperature the flesh softens within a few hours. Fishing boats usually cover the catch layer by layer with crushed ice, keeping the fish near zero degrees. The ratio of ice to fish is generally about one to one, and in hot weather or on longer voyages the share of ice is even higher.
p3_fishery_10: The depth of water in a fishing port rises and falls with the tide, and there are usually two high tides and two low tides in a day. Large fishing boats with deep drafts mostly enter and leave the port on a rising tide, so they do not run aground in the shallow parts of the channel. Because the tides come about fifty minutes later each day, the departure times of the boats shift later too, in a cycle of roughly half a month.
p3_gallery_01: The spring painting exhibition at a city art museum ran for 45 days and showed 128 oil paintings and watercolors. About 26 thousand visitors came in total, and average daily attendance on weekends was three times that on weekdays. On the twentieth day the museum printed two thousand more guide booklets, and after the exhibition closed, 9 works were lent to shows in other cities.
p3_gallery_02: The annual inspection record of a sculpture park lists 63 outdoor sculptures, 27 in bronze, 21 in stone and the other 15 in stainless steel. Eight of them showed surface rust spots or cracks, and a restoration team spent five weeks treating them. Fourteen new information signs were added around the lawns.
p3_gallery_03: The main exhibition hall on the second floor of the art museum is a rectangular space with pale gray walls. Track spotlights with adjustable angles line the ceiling, and two backless benches sit in the middle of the room. A white panel introducing the exhibition stands at the entrance, and the floor of polished concrete gives almost no echo underfoot.
p3_gallery_04: This bronze sculpture is about two meters tall and depicts an old man reading while seated on a rock. His head is slightly bowed, and his left hand holds the open pages of a book. The folds of his clothing are deeply cut, and after oxidation the surface has turned dark green. The base is a square block of granite whose corners have been worn smooth by rain.
p3_gallery_05: An oil painting goes through several steps on its way from the storeroom to the gallery. Staff first check its number and photograph it for the records, then inspect the painted surface and the frame for damage. The painting is packed into a custom wooden crate and moved to the gallery. After unpacking it rests for a day so the canvas can match the room temperature, and finally two people hang it on the wall together and level it.
p3_gallery_06: Making a stone carving usually starts with choosing the stone. The sculptor first shapes a small clay study, then marks key points on the block according to scale, and removes large pieces of excess stone with a power saw and chisels. The facial features and folds of clothing are refined step by step, and the surface is sanded from coarse to fine. The whole process can take several months.
p3_gallery_07: Last Thursday afternoon, a primary school pupil visiting an exhibition accidentally knocked over a sign stand in the gallery. As it fell, the stand struck the base of a nearby sculpture. Security staff immediately put up a temporary barrier. Conservators examined the sculpture and confirmed it was undamaged, the teacher leading the group apologized to the staff on the spot, and the gallery reopened half an hour later.
p3_gallery_08: The first solo exhibition of a young painter opened at a small gallery on the east side of the city. The twenty or so works on view all take the rooftops of an old neighborhood as their subject, mostly in grayish blue tones. More than a hundred visitors came on opening day, three paintings were bought by collectors in the first week, and the gallery extended the show by ten days as a result.
p3_gallery_09: When oil paintings are hung on gallery walls, the center of each picture is usually placed about 150 centimeters above the floor, close to the eye level of an adult visitor. Neighboring works are normally spaced at least 60 centimeters apart, and larger works are given a wider viewing distance in front, so that visitors do not crowd into one spot.
p3_gallery_10: The casting edition of a sculpture is one basis for judging its value. A bronze sculpture can be cast several times from the same mold, and artists usually limit the total, for example to eight casts. Each base is engraved with a number, and casts made beyond the set limit are generally not considered part of the original edition.
p3_garden_01: In early April, 56 rose plants were set out on the east side of the community garden, and 51 had survived by the end of the month. About eight in ten of the cosmos seeds sown at the same time came up, and the seedlings had already reached 15 centimeters in height. The garden was watered 9 times this month, and not at all during one week of heavy rain. Twelve lavender plants were added in the west corner of the flower bed.
p3_garden_06: This week the highest temperature in the glass greenhouse came on Thursday afternoon, at 31 degrees Celsius. The lowest came before dawn on Monday, at only 9 degrees Celsius. Daytime relative humidity was generally around 65 percent. Over the week the potted orchids produced 42 flowers, more than half of them on moth orchids.
p3_garden_02: This Japanese white pine bonsai has been tended for more than twenty years. Its trunk leans to the left, and the bends are covered with old, cracked bark. The branches have been pruned into layered, cloudlike pads, and the needles are short and dense. The pot is a shallow rectangular one of purple clay, with moss and a few small stones spread over the soil.
p3_garden_07: This courtyard garden covers only a little over forty square meters, with a winding flagstone path running through the middle. Plantain lilies and hydrangeas grow on both sides of the path, and in the corner stands an osmanthus tree taller than the eaves. A row of clay pots lines the foot of the east wall, holding mint and rosemary. At the far end of the yard sits a small water jar, with a few water lily leaves floating on its surface.
p3_garden_03: Before this pothos was repotted, the gardener held off watering for two days to let the soil dry a little. Next he tapped the sides of the pot and lifted the plant out together with its root ball. After the rotten roots were cut away, the plant went into a new pot one size larger, and fresh soil was packed in around it. Finally the pot was watered thoroughly and moved to a shady spot so the plant could recover.
p3_garden_08: After tomato seeds are sown, seedlings break through the soil in about five days. The first to open are two narrow seed leaves, and only after that do the toothed true leaves appear. When the seedlings reach about 15 centimeters, they are transplanted into the vegetable garden. A little over a month later, the plants gradually open pale yellow flowers, and once the flowers fall, the green fruit that forms slowly turns red.
p3_garden_04: One afternoon a few days ago, hail suddenly fell on the botanical garden on the west side of the city, lasting about ten minutes in all. A large patch of tulips in full bloom was snapped, and several glass panes in the greenhouse cracked. Staff worked through the night to clear away fallen leaves and broken twigs, and the next day they replanted the empty beds with petunias.
p3_garden_09: One evening in August, an epiphyllum bloomed on the balcony of a home on the old street. The bud began to unfold at about nine and was fully open by eleven, nearly 20 centimeters across. Neighbors caught the scent and came over one after another to look. By early the next morning, the flower had already closed and drooped.
p3_garden_05: Succulents have thick, fleshy leaves that can store a great deal of water. Most of them come from dry regions, so they tolerate drought but not waterlogging. When the potting soil stays wet for a long time, their roots rot easily. That is why most growers wait until the soil has dried out completely before watering again, and in winter the gaps between waterings grow even longer.
p3_garden_10: The flower color of hydrangeas changes with soil acidity. In acidic soil the plants take up aluminum more easily, and the flowers are mostly blue. When the soil is alkaline, aluminum is hard to absorb, and the flowers lean toward pink. Some gardeners bury sulfur powder in the soil so that the flowers gradually turn blue.
p3_geography_01: Observations from a hydrological station last year showed that the annual runoff of this river was about 32 billion cubic meters. The flood season ran from June to September, and these four months brought more than seventy percent of the yearly flow. The highest water level of the year came in the middle of July, 80 centimeters below the warning level. The lowest flow of the dry season occurred in February, when the river narrowed by nearly half.
p3_geography_02: A survey team set up 5 temperature stations on the southern slope of the mountain, at altitudes rising from 800 meters to 3200 meters. The average July temperature was 24 degrees at the foot of the slope and only 9 degrees at the highest point. The data showed that the temperature fell by about 6 degrees for every 1000 meters of elevation gained.
p3_geography_03: This delta is low and flat, and before reaching the sea the river splits into more than ten channels that spread toward the coast like open fingers. Between the channels lie broad rice fields and fish ponds, and villages are strung along the levees. Wide stands of reeds grow near the shore, and every autumn their plumes turn the tidal flats a pale gray.
p3_geography_04: This canyon is about 40 kilometers long, its rock walls rise several hundred meters on both sides, and the strata form alternating bands of reddish brown and pale gray. A swift river runs along the canyon floor, and the sound of the water echoes between the walls. Hardy shrubs that survive drought grow sparsely on the cliffs, and sunlight reaches the bottom only around midday.
p3_geography_05: An oxbow lake develops from a winding river channel. As a river flows across a plain, its outer bank is steadily eroded while sediment gradually builds up along the inner bank. The bend therefore grows tighter and tighter until the two ends of the channel almost meet. After a flood, the water cuts straight through the narrow neck, and the abandoned bend becomes a separate lake.
p3_geography_06: After winter sets in, the water temperature of northern rivers drops to around zero, and tiny ice crystals first appear on the surface. The crystals gather into thin plates of ice that drift downstream, while the ice along the banks slowly widens. As the air grows colder still, the floating pieces freeze together, and in the end the whole river is sealed under a sheet of ice.
p3_geography_07: Last summer, a surveying team measured the height of a snow mountain again. The members climbed in two groups to an observation point near the summit and set up satellite receivers. After three days of continuous measurement, the new elevation came out 2 meters lower than the earlier figure. Researchers attributed this mainly to thinner snow on the top.
p3_geography_08: In the autumn of the year before last, a dense fog lasting five days covered the coastal plain, and visibility at one point fell below 100 meters. During the fog, the port suspended ship arrivals and departures. Meteorologists later explained that the fog formed when warm, moist air flowed over the cooler sea surface. On the morning of the sixth day the wind shifted, and the fog quickly cleared.
p3_geography_09: When moist air meets a mountain range, it is forced to rise and gradually cools as it climbs. Once its temperature falls below the dew point, the water vapor condenses into clouds and produces precipitation. That is why windward slopes tend to receive more rain, while the air that crosses the summit becomes dry and the leeward slopes often stay arid.
p3_geography_10: The Mediterranean climate occurs mainly on the western coasts of continents between 30 and 40 degrees of latitude north and south. In summer these areas lie under subtropical high pressure, so the weather is hot and dry with little rain. In winter the westerly belt shifts toward lower latitudes, bringing mild and wet weather, and most of the yearly rainfall comes in this season.
p3_hotel_01: This seaside hotel has 126 guest rooms, and its average occupancy in the second week of July reached 92 percent. The breakfast hall served about 310 guests a day, with the peak around eight in the morning. During that week the front desk handled 41 late checkouts and 18 extra beds, and more than 200 pieces of luggage were stored.
p3_hotel_02: The housekeeping department scheduled 14 room attendants that day, and each cleaned an average of 15 rooms. A checked out room took about 35 minutes to clean, and a stayover room about 20 minutes. Over the day 380 sets of sheets and duvet covers were changed and nearly 900 toiletry items were restocked, and room inspections found broken light bulbs in 3 rooms, which were reported to the engineering department to be changed.
p3_hotel_03: The hotel lobby rises about ten meters, and a chandelier made of several hundred pieces of glass hangs from its center. The front desk is a single slab of light gray stone, and the wall behind it is inset with woven bamboo panels. Several groups of low fabric sofas stand on one side of the lobby, while beyond the floor to ceiling windows on the other side lies a courtyard planted with banana trees, where the afternoon sun slants in.
p3_hotel_04: This three day route sets out from an old town and follows a river valley upstream. The first night is spent at a timber inn by the river, and on the second day the route crosses a mountain pass more than one thousand meters above sea level, reaching a tea garden by evening. The last day passes two stone arch bridges and a field of rapeseed flowers, arriving back at the starting station in the afternoon.
p3_hotel_05: Checking in usually takes only a few minutes. The receptionist first looks up the booking and confirms the length of stay, then takes a deposit and prints a registration slip for the guest to sign. Next two key cards are made, and the guest is told the time and floor of breakfast. Finally a bellhop wheels a luggage cart to carry the cases into the room, draws back the curtains, and leaves.
p3_hotel_06: Turning over a checked out guest room begins with changing the linen. The attendant first opens the window to air the room and puts the used sheets and towels into a linen bag. Next comes the bathroom, wiped down from the basin all the way to the shower. When the bed is made, the duvet insert goes into its cover first and the pillows are placed after, with a folded blanket laid across the foot of the bed. Finally the tea bags and drinking water are restocked, and the door is locked after the lights are turned off.
p3_hotel_07: A tour group of twenty people had planned to check in at a mountaintop hotel in the early evening, but the mountain road was closed for repairs at short notice, and the coach waited halfway up the slope for two hours. On learning of the delay, the hotel moved dinner back to nine and kept hot soup warm. The group arrived at half past eight, and the key cards had already been sorted into envelopes by name and laid out neatly at the front desk.
p3_hotel_08: After a heavy rainstorm, water about twenty centimeters deep flowed into the underground car park of a riverside hotel. The engineering department ran three pumps through the night, and by four in the morning the water had mostly drained away. The next morning, the hotel contacted the owners of more than ten cars on the first basement level one by one and offered them a free car wash.
p3_hotel_09: Hotel room doors usually open inward, and an evacuation map is posted on the back of the door. The map marks the location of the room, as well as the two nearest emergency exits. Emergency lights are installed at intervals along the corridors, switching on automatically during a power cut and generally staying lit for no less than half an hour.
p3_hotel_10: Most hotels set checkout time at twelve noon, while check in starts after two in the afternoon. In the two hours between, the housekeeping department cleans and inspects the rooms. In the peak travel season rooms turn over tightly, so guests who arrive early often leave their luggage at the front desk first and collect their key cards once the rooms are ready.
p3_household_01: In October this family of three used 286 kilowatt hours of electricity, 54 fewer than in September. Most of the drop came from the air conditioner, while the fridge and the water heater used about the same as the month before. The washing machine ran 22 times this month, using about 50 liters of water each time, and its drying function was used only 3 times.
p3_household_02: The Saturday cleaning lasted from nine in the morning until one in the afternoon. The family scrubbed six windows and two mirrors and cleared out three bags of old newspapers and a box of shoes no longer worn. The range hood filter soaked for 40 minutes before it came clean, 7 bottles of expired seasonings were thrown out of the fridge, and finally the floor was mopped twice, leaving the rooms much brighter.
p3_household_03: This south facing living room is under twenty square meters, with walls painted off white. A long table in light wood stands by the window, holding a pot of golden pothos and a ceramic pen holder. On the low cabinet opposite the sofa sit a television and a few photo albums, a round gray blue rug covers the floor, and a wrought iron floor lamp stands in the corner.
p3_household_04: The front loading washing machine in the corner of the balcony has a white body and a round glass door on the front. Above the door is a row of knobs and buttons offering more than ten wash programs. The drawer in the upper left corner is divided into two small compartments, holding detergent and fabric softener respectively. Four height adjustable feet sit under the base, and the machine barely shakes while running.
p3_household_05: Cleaning the indoor unit of an air conditioner is usually done by a technician on a home visit. He first cuts the power, lifts open the front panel, takes out the two filters, rinses them with clean water, and leaves them to dry in a shady spot. Next he brushes the cooling fins lightly with a soft brush, then wipes the vanes of the air outlet clean with a damp cloth. Once the filters are completely dry they go back in place, and the job ends after a ten minute trial run with the power on.
p3_household_06: Every Sunday, this family tidies the wardrobe. All the clothes are first taken out and spread on the bed, then sorted into three piles by thickness. Heavy coats that are seldom worn go into vacuum storage bags, which are pressed flat and placed on the top shelf. Shirts for the current season are hung from light to dark, while socks and scarves are rolled up and tucked into the compartments of a drawer.
p3_household_07: A household fridge suddenly stopped cooling in the middle of the night, and by the next morning the ice in the freezer had begun to melt. The owner contacted the after sales service, a repairman came that afternoon to inspect it, and he found that the thermostat had worn out and failed. Changing the part took twenty minutes, and once the fridge was running again, the freezer dropped back to minus eighteen degrees within three hours.
p3_household_08: The drain hose of a washing machine in an upstairs flat came loose, and water seeped through gaps in the floor into the ceiling below. The downstairs residents noticed a yellow water stain on their ceiling and went upstairs to knock and explain. The upstairs residents shut off the water valve at once and refastened the drain hose, and a week later they hired a worker to repaint the ceiling downstairs.
p3_household_09: The fresh food compartment of a fridge is usually set to about 4 degrees, a temperature at which food keeps longer. The upper shelves are slightly warmer and are often used for cooked food and leftovers. The lower shelves are the coldest and suit fresh meat and fish. The door racks take in warm air every time the door opens, so their temperature varies the most, and they usually hold drinks and condiments.
p3_household_10: The moisture content of a wooden floor changes with the humidity of the air, so an expansion gap of about one centimeter is usually left between the boards and the wall during installation.
